name: End-reversing outrigger sailing
summary: CHamoru sailors reversed direction by making the stern of their outrigger canoe the new bow, keeping the float on the windward side instead of turning the boat.
description: Sailors change the direction of a sailing canoe with a lateral stabilizing float by making the previous stern the bow; documented forms transfer a sail or yard to the other end. This offers a different manoeuvre from turning a fixed-bow craft through the wind.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

date.label: 1521 CE
date.basis: Pigafetta’s narrated encounter with Mariana Islanders, as dated in the University of Guam history.

events.statement: In 1521 CHamoru islanders used sailing canoes with an attached lateral float whose ends could interchange.
events.scope: An outrigger sailing canoe whose bow and stern can interchange; the observed 1521 vessel had a lateral stabilizing float and a sewn palm-leaf sail.
events.population: CHamoru sailors encountered by the Magellan expedition
events.caveats: The 1521 account does not explain how its sail was shifted, date the manoeuvre’s origin, or establish that every Mariana craft shared the same rig.

evidence.supports: The account describes islanders sailing small outrigger boats with palm-leaf sails and interchangeable ends.
The University of Guam history dates Pigafetta’s description to 1521 and identifies the offshore canoe context.

date.label: 1686 CE
date.basis: Dampier’s Guam visit in the 1697 narrative.

events.statement: In 1686 Dampier described CHamoru sailors changing direction by shifting the yard to the opposite end of an outrigger canoe.
events.scope: A late seventeenth-century double-ended CHamoru sailing hull with one stabilizing float; the crew shifted the yard when reversing ends.
events.population: CHamoru sailors observed by William Dampier
events.caveats: The later description is a separate witness; it does not prove the precise rig on the canoes observed in 1521. Dampier’s side-to-wind account differs from later descriptions.

evidence.locator: Guam, paragraph beginning “The natives are very ingenious”
evidence.supports: Dampier describes the double-ended outrigger canoe, yard shift and its role in changing direction.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Pigafetta’s narrated encounter with Mariana Islanders, as dated in the University of Guam history. The 1521 account does not explain how its sail was shifted, date the manoeuvre’s origin, or establish that every Mariana craft shared the same rig. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.community: CHamoru sailors encountered in the Mariana Islands in 1521
community_entry.rationale: An observed sailing use with reversible ends gives a bounded community-entry witness. Linguistic reconstruction points to an earlier, not precisely dated Oceanic history.
community_entry.caveats: This is not a claim that the technique originated in the Marianas in 1521. The observed account does not show sail shifting; the 1686 source separately describes a yard shift. Rig ancestry and exact invention chronology remain unresolved.
